hints: Focus on what you are actually adding to the culture solution: sodium chloride dissolves to add lots of solute particles, so think about how more solute changes water potential.
Remember water always moves by osmosis from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential, so compare the freshwater cell sap with the now salty outside solution.
walkthrough:
**What does adding salt do to water potential?**

Pure water has a water potential of $0 \text{ kPa}$, the highest possible value. Adding any solute lowers it, making it negative.

Key rule:
$$\text{more solute} = \text{more negative solute potential} = \text{more negative water potential}$$

**Which way will water move?**

These are freshwater single-celled plant cells, so their cell sap is much less salty than the new culture solution. That means the cells start with a higher (less negative) water potential than the solution outside.

Water moves down its gradient, so water leaves the cells by osmosis into the more negative solution.

**What happens to the cells after 5 minutes?**

As water leaves, the vacuole and cytoplasm shrink and the cell surface membrane pulls away from the cell wall. This is plasmolysis, the opposite of becoming turgid. So the solution becomes more negative and the cells become plasmolysed.

options.A: Adding solute cannot make water potential less negative (higher), it always lowers it, although plasmolysed is the correct cell change.
options.B: Both parts are wrong here, adding salt lowers water potential and water leaving the cell cannot make it turgid.
options.C: Correct and reassuring: more solute makes the solution more negative, so water leaves the freshwater cells by osmosis and they become plasmolysed.
options.D: More negative solution is correct, but the cells will lose water and shrink, not gain water to become turgid.
